items.stem: The European heatwave of summer 2003 is estimated to have caused about how many deaths?
items.answer: About 70,000
items.markingKey: About 70,000. Most victims were elderly people in France, Italy and Spain.

items.stem: Explain the difference between thermal expansion and ice-sheet melt.
items.answer: Thermal expansion raises sea level as warming water expands; ice-sheet melt adds water from land-based ice (Greenland, Antarctica) to the oceans; both contribute, with ice melt becoming more important.
items.markingKey: Thermal expansion raises sea level as warming water expands; ice-sheet melt adds water from land-based ice (Greenland, Antarctica) to the oceans; both contribute, with ice melt becoming more important. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how climate change can threaten food security.
items.answer: Higher temperatures and droughts reduce yields of maize and wheat; changing rainfall disrupts growing seasons; extreme events destroy crops; pests and diseases spread; price spikes reduce access for the poor.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher temperatures and droughts reduce yields of maize and wheat; changing rainfall disrupts growing seasons; extreme events destroy crops; pests and diseases spread; price spikes reduce access for the poor. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A cooperative growing rice in Vietnam harvested 2,462 t from 637 ha in 2005 and 3,741 t from the same area in 2020. Calculate the yield (t/ha) in each year and the percentage change in yield.
Isabel writes: "Sea level is rising by the same amount everywhere." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Relative sea-level rise varies with subsidence, uplift, ocean currents and gravity effects; Jakarta and Manila experience much faster relative rise than the global mean.
items.markingKey: Relative sea-level rise varies with subsidence, uplift, ocean currents and gravity effects; Jakarta and Manila experience much faster relative rise than the global mean. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
The following information is provided.

Table: global mean sea level rise rate (IPCC AR6, mm per year) - 1901-1971: 1.3; 1971-2006: 1.9; 2006-2018: 3.7.

Calculate the total rise implied over a century at the 2006-2018 rate.
items.answer: 3.7 mm × 100 = 370 mm ≈ 0.37 m (if the rate stays constant, which is unlikely as it is accelerating).
items.markingKey: 3.7 mm × 100 = 370 mm ≈ 0.37 m (if the rate stays constant, which is unlikely as it is accelerating). Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [4]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: "Sea-level rise is the most serious consequence of climate change for people." Discuss this statement, with reference to examples you have studied.
items.answer: Sea-level rise is the gravest long-term threat for coastal places, but for most people heat, water and food impacts are more immediate.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: threatens hundreds of millions in low-lying coasts and deltas; existential threat to small island states such as Tuvalu and the Maldives. Against / limitations: heat, drought and food insecurity affect more people now; sea-level rise is slow and can be partly adapted to (Netherlands). A supported conclusion might be: Sea-level rise is the gravest long-term threat for coastal places, but for most people heat, water and food impacts are more immediate. items.stem: Examine the impacts of climate change on water and food security in contrasting places.
items.answer: Indicative content: Located examples (Sahel, Pakistan, Andes, Bangladesh, Canada), mechanisms, data and scale; recognition of uneven impacts; judgement.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "When all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food (FAO, 1996)"?
items.answer: food security
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of food security.

items.stem: Explain why a warmer climate is expected to increase the intensity of extreme rainfall.
items.answer: Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapour per °C, so storms can produce heavier downpours, increasing flash-flood risk.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapour per °C, so storms can produce heavier downpours, increasing flash-flood risk. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Sea level is rising by the same amount everywhere." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Relative sea-level rise varies with subsidence, uplift, ocean currents and gravity effects; Jakarta and Manila experience much faster relative rise than the global mean.
items.markingKey: Relative sea-level rise varies with subsidence, uplift, ocean currents and gravity effects; Jakarta and Manila experience much faster relative rise than the global mean. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between impacts on food access and impacts on food availability.
items.answer: Availability concerns how much food is produced (yields, harvests); access concerns whether people can afford or obtain it (prices, incomes) - climate shocks can affect both.
items.markingKey: Availability concerns how much food is produced (yields, harvests); access concerns whether people can afford or obtain it (prices, incomes) - climate shocks can affect both. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Tide-gauge records at Miami show mean sea level of 6999 mm (relative to a local datum) in 1993 and 7187 mm in 2013. Calculate the mean rate of relative sea-level rise. Project the additional rise over the next 75 years at this rate, and explain why the rate here may differ from the global mean (about 3.7 mm/yr recently).
items.answer: 9.4 mm/yr; ≈ 70 cm in 75 years; local subsidence (groundwater pumping, delta compaction), tectonics or ocean circulation alter relative rise.
items.markingKey: A1 9.4 mm/yr; A1 705 mm; R1 R1 relative vs eustatic explanation.

items.stem: Suggest two ways that sea-level rise could affect the economy of Bangladesh.
items.answer: Loss of farmland to flooding and salinisation, reducing rice output; damage to infrastructure and displacement of coastal communities, increasing rural-urban migration to Dhaka.
items.markingKey: Loss of farmland to flooding and salinisation, reducing rice output; damage to infrastructure and displacement of coastal communities, increasing rural-urban migration to Dhaka.

items.stem: Israel has total renewable water resources of about 1.78 km³ per year and a population of about 9.7 million. Calculate the renewable water available per person (m³ per year) and classify it using the Falkenmark indicator (1,700 / 1,000 / 500 m³). If the population grows to 12.6 million with no change in supply, what would the new figure be?
items.answer: 184 m³/person/yr (absolute water scarcity); future 141 m³/person/yr
items.markingKey: M1 km³ × 10⁹ ÷ population; A1 184 m³; R1 absolute water scarcity; A1 141 m³.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that climate change impacts on food security will be greatest in low-latitude countries? Refer to places and scales you have studied.
items.answer: Low-latitude, low-income countries face the largest impacts because of exposure and vulnerability, though global markets spread effects.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: tropical crops are already near heat thresholds; Sahel and South Asia yields fall; high dependence on rain-fed agriculture and low adaptive capacity. Arguments challenging it: global food prices transmit shocks everywhere; mid-latitude breadbaskets face drought (2010 Russia, 2012 USA). Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Low-latitude, low-income countries face the largest impacts because of exposure and vulnerability, though global markets spread effects. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Map description: projected change in maize yields by 2050 (%) - Southern Africa −15 to −25; West Africa −10 to −20; South Asia −5 to −15; northern USA 0 to −10; Canadian prairies +5 to +10.

(a) Describe the pattern of projected change. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest why the largest losses are projected for southern Africa. [6]
items.answer: (a) Largest losses in low-latitude regions (southern and West Africa); smaller losses in mid-latitudes; gains only in high-latitude Canada. (b) Crops are already near temperature thresholds; increased drought frequency; reliance on rain-fed maize; limited irrigation and adaptive capacity.
items.markingKey: (a) Largest losses in low-latitude regions (southern and West Africa); smaller losses in mid-latitudes; gains only in high-latitude Canada. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "exposure"?
options: The presence of people, livelihoods and assets in places that could be affected by a hazard
Reliable access to an acceptable quantity and quality of water for health, livelihoods and production, with acceptable water-related risks
Movement of people driven wholly or partly by climate-related changes such as drought, sea-level rise or extreme events
The increase in mean sea level caused mainly by thermal expansion of seawater and melting of glaciers and ice sheets
items.answer: The presence of people, livelihoods and assets in places that could be affected by a hazard
items.markingKey: A. "exposure" is the presence of people, livelihoods and assets in places that could be affected by a hazard.

items.stem: Explain the difference between exposure and vulnerability.
items.answer: Exposure is being in the path of a hazard; vulnerability is the susceptibility to harm once exposed - two people equally exposed can have very different vulnerability.
items.markingKey: Exposure is being in the path of a hazard; vulnerability is the susceptibility to harm once exposed - two people equally exposed can have very different vulnerability. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the elderly and very young are particularly vulnerable to heatwaves.
items.answer: They have weaker thermoregulation, more chronic illness and are more dependent on others; isolation and lack of air-conditioning raise risk.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They have weaker thermoregulation, more chronic illness and are more dependent on others; isolation and lack of air-conditioning raise risk. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to Mumbai's 2005 flood, explain how it illustrates the uneven vulnerability of urban populations.
items.answer: About 944 mm of rain in 24 hours flooded informal settlements along blocked drains and the Mithi River. Poor drainage and informal housing in exposed locations raised impacts for the urban poor.
items.markingKey: Context (About 944 mm of rain in 24 hours flooded informal settlements along blocked drains and the Mithi River.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Poor drainage and informal housing in exposed locations raised impacts for the urban poor. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the uneven vulnerability of urban populations.

items.stem: Suggest why smallholder farmers in the Sahel are highly vulnerable to drought.
items.answer: They depend on rain-fed crops and livestock, have little irrigation, savings or insurance, and face land degradation and insecurity.
items.markingKey: They depend on rain-fed crops and livestock, have little irrigation, savings or insurance, and face land degradation and insecurity.

items.stem: Examine why the impacts of climate change are unequal between and within countries.
items.answer: Indicative content: Exposure vs vulnerability; poverty, gender, age, location; examples at two scales (Katrina, Bangladesh, Sahel, 2003 heatwave); judgement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Exposure vs vulnerability; poverty, gender, age, location; examples at two scales (Katrina, Bangladesh, Sahel, 2003 heatwave); judgement. items.stem: Omar writes: "High-income countries are not vulnerable to climate change." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Exposed and marginalised groups in rich countries suffer badly (Katrina 2005, the 2003 European heatwave, 2021 heat dome).
items.markingKey: Exposed and marginalised groups in rich countries suffer badly (Katrina 2005, the 2003 European heatwave, 2021 heat dome). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between resilience and vulnerability.
items.answer: Vulnerability is susceptibility to harm; resilience is the ability to absorb, recover and adapt - reducing vulnerability builds resilience.
items.markingKey: Vulnerability is susceptibility to harm; resilience is the ability to absorb, recover and adapt - reducing vulnerability builds resilience. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why vulnerability can differ greatly within a single city.
items.answer: Informal settlements on steep slopes or floodplains, lack of drainage and services, and low incomes contrast with protected, wealthier districts - e.g. Mumbai's slums in the 2005 floods.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Informal settlements on steep slopes or floodplains, lack of drainage and services, and low incomes contrast with protected, wealthier districts - e.g. Mumbai's slums in the 2005 floods. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

Describe the differences shown.
items.answer: Deaths ranged from about 138,000 in Myanmar to 1,800 in the USA and just 1 in Australia despite comparable intensities.
items.markingKey: Deaths ranged from about 138,000 in Myanmar to 1,800 in the USA and just 1 in Australia despite comparable intensities. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (5.6 − 6.5) ÷ 6.5 × 100; A1 -13.8% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: To what extent is it true that those who have contributed least to climate change are the most vulnerable to it? Refer to places and scales you have studied.
items.answer: Broadly true at the global scale, which underpins climate justice arguments and the loss-and-damage fund.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: least-developed countries emit a small share of CO₂ but suffer severe impacts (Bangladesh, Sahel, Pacific islands); within countries, the poor emit least but are most exposed. Arguments challenging it: high emitters such as Australia and the USA also suffer severe impacts; vulnerability depends on governance and adaptation. Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Broadly true at the global scale, which underpins climate justice arguments and the loss-and-damage fund. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A dispute or violence linked to competition for scarce resources such as water or grazing land"?
items.answer: resource conflict
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of resource conflict.

items.stem: Explain why the link between climate change and conflict is debated.
items.answer: Conflict has many causes (politics, ethnicity, governance, economics); climate may contribute through drought and resource scarcity, but evidence is mixed and attributing a war to climate risks ignoring human responsibility, e.g. the debate over the 2006-10 Syrian drought.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Conflict has many causes (politics, ethnicity, governance, economics); climate may contribute through drought and resource scarcity, but evidence is mixed and attributing a war to climate risks ignoring human responsibility, e.g. the debate over the 2006-10 Syrian drought. items.stem:

Text: "Groundswell (World Bank, 2021) projects that, without action, up to 216 million people could be internal climate migrants by 2050, including 86 million in sub-Saharan Africa and 40 million in South Asia."

Calculate the share of the projected total in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia combined.
items.markingKey: (86 + 40)/216 × 100 = 58.3% Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [2]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Suggest two health impacts of more frequent heatwaves in South Asian cities.
items.answer: Heatstroke deaths among outdoor workers; worsening cardiovascular and respiratory illness; reduced labour productivity; water-borne disease when supplies fail.
items.markingKey: Heatstroke deaths among outdoor workers; worsening cardiovascular and respiratory illness; reduced labour productivity; water-borne disease when supplies fail.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that describing climate change as a threat multiplier helps governments respond effectively.
items.answer: The concept is useful if it promotes adaptation and development rather than militarised responses.
items.markingKey: For: links climate to security encourages funding and planning. Against: risks securitising migrants and justifying border controls. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Define the term "vector-borne disease".
items.answer: An illness transmitted by organisms such as mosquitoes or ticks, e.g. malaria and dengue, whose range is affected by climate
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an illness transmitted by organisms such as mosquitoes or ticks, e.g. malaria and dengue, whose range is affected by climate. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between slow-onset climate impacts and sudden-onset climate impacts.
items.answer: Slow-onset impacts (sea-level rise, desertification, glacier retreat) build over years and lead to gradual migration; sudden-onset events (floods, cyclones) cause rapid, often temporary displacement.
items.markingKey: Slow-onset impacts (sea-level rise, desertification, glacier retreat) build over years and lead to gradual migration; sudden-onset events (floods, cyclones) cause rapid, often temporary displacement. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which the spread of malaria in the East African highlands shows climate impacts on health.
items.answer: Cases have appeared at higher altitudes in Ethiopia and Kenya as temperatures rose. Warming allows disease vectors to survive in previously cool places.
items.markingKey: Context (Cases have appeared at higher altitudes in Ethiopia and Kenya as temperatures rose.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "food security"?
options: A dispute or violence linked to competition for scarce resources such as water or grazing land
A weather event that is rare at a particular place and time of year, such as a severe heatwave, flood or tropical cyclone
The degree to which people or places are susceptible to harm from a hazard and unable to cope, shaped by poverty, location, age, gender and governance
When all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food (FAO, 1996)
items.answer: When all people at all times have physical and economic access to sufficient, safe and nutritious food (FAO, 1996)

items.stem: In Hurricane Katrina (2005), which New Orleans neighbourhood with a mainly low-income African-American population was devastated by levee failure?
items.answer: The Lower Ninth Ward

items.stem: By about how much has the surface area of Lake Chad shrunk since the 1960s?
items.answer: About 90%
items.markingKey: C. The lake shrank from about 25,000 km² to under 2,000 km² due to drought and irrigation.

items.stem: Leila writes: "Everyone in a country faces the same climate risk." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Risk varies with location, income, age, gender, health and social networks, so impacts are highly uneven within countries.
items.markingKey: Risk varies with location, income, age, gender, health and social networks, so impacts are highly uneven within countries. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Millions of climate refugees are already protected by international law." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: There is no legal category of "climate refugee"; such migrants rely on national policies or regional agreements.

items.stem: Explain why most climate-related migration is internal and short-distance.
items.answer: Most people move to nearby towns or cities temporarily; international migration needs money, documents and networks that the poorest lack, and many prefer to stay close to land and family.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that those who have contributed least to climate change are the most vulnerable to it?
items.answer: Broadly true at the global scale, which underpins climate justice arguments and the loss-and-damage fund.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: least-developed countries emit a small share of CO₂ but suffer severe impacts (Bangladesh, Sahel, Pacific islands); within countries, the poor emit least but are most exposed. Against / limitations: high emitters such as Australia and the USA also suffer severe impacts; vulnerability depends on governance and adaptation. A supported conclusion might be: Broadly true at the global scale, which underpins climate justice arguments and the loss-and-damage fund. items.stem: Examine the ways in which climate change can increase risks to human health and security.
items.answer: Indicative content: Heat, disease vectors, food/water insecurity, displacement, conflict; named examples (Lake Chad, Syria, East Africa, Pacific); debate on attribution; judgement.

items.stem: "Sea-level rise is the most serious consequence of climate change for people." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Sea-level rise is the gravest long-term threat for coastal places, but for most people heat, water and food impacts are more immediate.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - arguments supporting the statement: threatens hundreds of millions in low-lying coasts and deltas; existential threat to small island states such as Tuvalu and the Maldives. Arguments challenging it: heat, drought and food insecurity affect more people now; sea-level rise is slow and can be partly adapted to (Netherlands). Evaluation should weigh places, scales, perspectives and time. Judgement: Sea-level rise is the gravest long-term threat for coastal places, but for most people heat, water and food impacts are more immediate. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Survey of 50 households in a Dhaka informal settlement after a 2023 flood: households with no savings 34; households with a member unable to work for over a week 21; households receiving no warning 28.

(a) Calculate the percentage of households with no savings and with no warning. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain how these factors increase vulnerability. [6]
items.answer: (a) No savings 68%; no warning 56% (b) No savings means households cannot recover or rebuild quickly; lack of warning prevents moving people and assets, raising losses.
items.markingKey: (a) No savings 68%; no warning 56% (b) No savings means households cannot recover or rebuild quickly; lack of warning prevents moving people and assets, raising losses. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). Infographic markscheme [10]: part (a) [4] - award 1 mark per valid point taken from the resource (data must be quoted with units for full marks); part (b) [6] - up to 2 marks for each developed explanation linking the resource to own knowledge; reward named examples; maximum 3 marks if the resource is not used.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "extreme weather event".
items.answer: A weather event that is rare at a particular place and time of year, such as a severe heatwave, flood or tropical cyclone
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a weather event that is rare at a particular place and time of year, such as a severe heatwave, flood or tropical cyclone. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Define the term "adaptive capacity".
items.answer: The ability of a system or community to adjust to climate change, moderate damage and take advantage of opportunities
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the ability of a system or community to adjust to climate change, moderate damage and take advantage of opportunities. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "planned relocation"?
options: An illness transmitted by organisms such as mosquitoes or ticks, e.g. malaria and dengue, whose range is affected by climate
The increase in volume of seawater as it warms, a major contributor to sea-level rise
The organised movement of a community away from a high-risk area, e.g. coastal villages in Fiji
Movement of people driven wholly or partly by climate-related changes such as drought, sea-level rise or extreme events
items.answer: The organised movement of a community away from a high-risk area, e.g. coastal villages in Fiji
items.markingKey: C. "planned relocation" is the organised movement of a community away from a high-risk area, e.g. coastal villages in Fiji.

items.stem: Kwame writes: "Melting sea ice is a major cause of sea-level rise." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Sea ice already floats, so its melting barely changes sea level; land ice and thermal expansion are the main causes.
items.markingKey: Sea ice already floats, so its melting barely changes sea level; land ice and thermal expansion are the main causes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between vulnerability and resilience.
items.answer: Vulnerability is susceptibility to harm; resilience is the ability to absorb, recover and adapt - reducing vulnerability builds resilience.
items.markingKey: Vulnerability is susceptibility to harm; resilience is the ability to absorb, recover and adapt - reducing vulnerability builds resilience. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Climate change was the sole cause of the Syrian civil war." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The 2006-10 drought may have added to rural hardship and migration, but repression, governance failure and politics were the main causes.
items.markingKey: The 2006-10 drought may have added to rural hardship and migration, but repression, governance failure and politics were the main causes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between ice-sheet melt and thermal expansion.
items.answer: Thermal expansion raises sea level as warming water expands; ice-sheet melt adds water from land-based ice (Greenland, Antarctica) to the oceans; both contribute, with ice melt becoming more important.
items.markingKey: Thermal expansion raises sea level as warming water expands; ice-sheet melt adds water from land-based ice (Greenland, Antarctica) to the oceans; both contribute, with ice melt becoming more important. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why women can be more vulnerable than men to some climate hazards.
items.answer: In some societies women have less access to warnings, swimming skills, land titles and credit, and caring roles and clothing norms limit evacuation, as in the 1991 Bangladesh cyclone where female death rates were much higher.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In some societies women have less access to warnings, swimming skills, land titles and credit, and caring roles and clothing norms limit evacuation, as in the 1991 Bangladesh cyclone where female death rates were much higher. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between refugees and climate migrants.
items.answer: Refugees are legally protected under the 1951 Convention because of persecution or conflict; people moving because of climate change have no specific legal status and are mostly internal migrants.
items.markingKey: Refugees are legally protected under the 1951 Convention because of persecution or conflict; people moving because of climate change have no specific legal status and are mostly internal migrants. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A cooperative growing soybeans in Brazil (Mato Grosso) harvested 2,191 t from 880 ha in 2005 and 3,092 t from the same area in 2020. Calculate the yield (t/ha) in each year and the percentage change in yield.
Briefly describe the 2003 European heatwave in Paris and explain what it reveals about age and social isolation as vulnerability factors.
items.answer: Many of the victims were elderly people living alone in top-floor apartments. Physiological sensitivity and isolation raised mortality among older people.
items.markingKey: Context (Many of the victims were elderly people living alone in top-floor apartments.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Physiological sensitivity and isolation raised mortality among older people. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to age and social isolation as vulnerability factors.

items.stem: The UAE (population 10 million) has a natural increase of 9.8 per 1,000. In one year it received 467 thousand immigrants and 382 thousand people emigrated. Calculate the net migration rate and the overall rate of population change per 1,000, and state which component dominates.
items.answer: net migration +8.5 per 1,000; total change +18.3 per 1,000; dominant component: natural change
items.markingKey: A1 +8.5; M1 natural change + net migration; A1 +18.3; R1 natural change.

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Map description: projected change in maize yields by 2050 (%) - Southern Africa −15 to −25; West Africa −10 to −20; South Asia −5 to −15; northern USA 0 to −10; Canadian prairies +5 to +10.

Suggest why the largest losses are projected for southern Africa.
items.answer: Crops are already near temperature thresholds; increased drought frequency; reliance on rain-fed maize; limited irrigation and adaptive capacity.
items.markingKey: Crops are already near temperature thresholds; increased drought frequency; reliance on rain-fed maize; limited irrigation and adaptive capacity. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: A data table shows the area of Arctic summer (September) sea ice measured by a polar research centre: 1990 - 6.9 million km²; 2000 - 5.2 million km². Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (5.2 − 6.9) ÷ 6.9 × 100; A1 -24.6% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Briefly describe the spread of malaria in the East African highlands and explain what it reveals about climate impacts on health.
items.answer: Cases have appeared at higher altitudes in Ethiopia and Kenya as temperatures rose. Warming allows disease vectors to survive in previously cool places.
items.markingKey: Context (Cases have appeared at higher altitudes in Ethiopia and Kenya as temperatures rose.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Warming allows disease vectors to survive in previously cool places. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to climate impacts on health.

items.stem: A data table shows the number of days above 35 °C per year in an Australian inland town: 1990 - 54.2 days; 2005 - 62.2 days. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (62.2 − 54.2) ÷ 54.2 × 100; A1 +14.8% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that poverty is the most important factor determining vulnerability to climate change.
items.answer: Poverty is the strongest underlying factor, but it interacts with location, demographic and social factors.
items.markingKey: For: the poor live in exposed places with weak housing and few assets. Against: age, gender, disability and isolation matter even in rich places (2003 heatwave). [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that describing climate change as a threat multiplier helps governments respond effectively.
items.answer: The concept is useful if it promotes adaptation and development rather than militarised responses.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: links climate to security encourages funding and planning; highlights vulnerable regions (Sahel, Lake Chad). Against / limitations: risks securitising migrants and justifying border controls; can distract from political causes of conflict. A supported conclusion might be: The concept is useful if it promotes adaptation and development rather than militarised responses. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that climate change impacts on food security will be greatest in low-latitude countries.
items.answer: Low-latitude, low-income countries face the largest impacts because of exposure and vulnerability, though global markets spread effects.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: tropical crops are already near heat thresholds; Sahel and South Asia yields fall; high dependence on rain-fed agriculture and low adaptive capacity. Against / limitations: global food prices transmit shocks everywhere; mid-latitude breadbaskets face drought (2010 Russia, 2012 USA). A supported conclusion might be: Low-latitude, low-income countries face the largest impacts because of exposure and vulnerability, though global markets spread effects. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: deaths from tropical cyclones of similar strength - Cyclone Nargis, Myanmar 2008: about 138,000; Hurricane Katrina, USA 2005: about 1,800; Cyclone Yasi, Australia 2011: 1.

(a) Describe the differences shown. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest two reasons for the differences. [6]
items.answer: (a) Deaths ranged from about 138,000 in Myanmar to 1,800 in the USA and just 1 in Australia despite comparable intensities. (b) Warning systems and evacuation capacity (Australia), poverty and housing quality, governance (Myanmar initially restricted aid), exposure of the Irrawaddy delta population.

(b) Warning systems and evacuation capacity (Australia), poverty and housing quality, governance (Myanmar initially restricted aid), exposure of the Irrawaddy delta population. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b).
